prompt: A variable holding a running total is in use while a program runs. Where does it live?
optionA: On disk, since the program was loaded from disk
optionB: In working memory, and it is lost when the program ends
optionC: On disk, because totals are important
optionD: In both places at once
correctAnswerText: In working memory, and it is lost when the program ends
explanation: A value a program is using sits in working memory. Nothing puts it on disk unless the program deliberately writes it there.

prompt: A machine loses power while a program is running. What is lost?
optionA: Everything, including files already saved
optionB: Nothing, since the machine will restore its state
optionC: Only the program itself
optionD: Whatever was only in working memory
correctAnswerText: Whatever was only in working memory
explanation: Working memory does not survive without power and storage does. Files already written are unaffected.

prompt: A document is opened in an editor and changed but not saved. Where do the changes exist?
optionA: In working memory only
optionB: In storage, since the file was opened from there
optionC: In both, since editors save continuously
optionD: Nowhere until the editor is closed
correctAnswerText: In working memory only
explanation: The unsaved changes have not reached the file. Saving is what copies them from working memory into storage.

prompt: Why is working memory used at all, when storage is much larger?
optionA: Because storage cannot hold running programs
optionB: Because working memory is more reliable
optionC: Because it is far quicker to reach, which is what a running program needs
optionD: Because storage is only used for backups
correctAnswerText: Because it is far quicker to reach, which is what a running program needs
explanation: Speed is the whole reason for the arrangement. Storage could hold everything and would be far too slow to work from directly.

prompt: A student says a file of two gigabytes cannot be processed on a machine with one gigabyte of working memory. What is wrong with the claim?
optionA: Nothing; the file will not fit and cannot be processed
optionB: The file can be processed a piece at a time, so the whole of it need never be in memory at once
optionC: The file can be processed because memory expands as needed
optionD: The claim is right unless the file is compressed
correctAnswerText: The file can be processed a piece at a time, so the whole of it need never be in memory at once
explanation: Only what is held simultaneously has to fit. Reading a line, dealing with it and moving on keeps the requirement tiny however large the file is.

prompt: A value is needed only while one function call is in progress. Which region suits it?
optionA: The region for values outliving the call
optionB: Storage, since the value is temporary
optionC: Either; the choice makes no difference
optionD: The region tied to the call, released when the call returns
correctAnswerText: The region tied to the call, released when the call returns
explanation: Lifetime is what decides. A value needed only for the duration of a call belongs where it is released automatically at the end of it.

prompt: A value must still exist after the call that created it has returned. Which region suits it?
optionA: The region for values whose lifetime is not tied to a call
optionB: The region tied to the call
optionC: Storage, since it must survive
optionD: Either; the value survives regardless
correctAnswerText: The region for values whose lifetime is not tied to a call
explanation: The call-tied region is released when the call ends, which would take the value with it. Outliving a call means living somewhere the call does not control.

prompt: What decides which of the two regions a value belongs in?
optionA: How large it is
optionB: What type it has
optionC: How long it must last
optionD: How often it is used
correctAnswerText: How long it must last
explanation: Lifetime is the criterion. A small value that must outlive its call belongs in the longer-lived region, and a large one that need not can sit in the call-tied one.

prompt: A student says large values always belong in the longer-lived region and small ones in the call-tied region. What is wrong with the rule?
optionA: Nothing; size is the correct criterion
optionB: It uses size where lifetime is what matters, so it gets small long-lived values wrong
optionC: It is right except for values of exactly one byte
optionD: It is right for numbers and wrong for text
correctAnswerText: It uses size where lifetime is what matters, so it gets small long-lived values wrong
explanation: The rule happens to work often, because large things are frequently long-lived. It fails exactly where the two criteria disagree, and those are the cases that cause faults.

prompt: Two programs are running, and each holds a value at what it reports as the same address. Are they referring to the same memory?
optionA: Yes, since the addresses are identical
optionB: Yes, if the two programs were started together
optionC: It cannot be determined
optionD: No; each program has its own addresses
correctAnswerText: No; each program has its own addresses
explanation: The addresses a program sees are its own, and identical numbers in two programs point at different physical memory. This is what makes isolation possible rather than magical.

prompt: A program prints an address and a developer wants to inspect that location from another program. What is the difficulty?
optionA: The address means something only within the program that printed it
optionB: Addresses cannot be printed
optionC: The address will have changed by the time it is read
optionD: There is no difficulty; the address is universal
correctAnswerText: The address means something only within the program that printed it
explanation: Handing the number to another program hands it a number that means something else there. Inspecting it requires going through the first program.

prompt: What does a program address actually refer to?
optionA: A fixed location in the physical memory chips
optionB: A position on disk
optionC: A location within that program own view of memory
optionD: A position in the list of running programs
correctAnswerText: A location within that program own view of memory
explanation: The program view is translated to physical memory by the system, and the program never sees the physical location. That translation is what keeps programs apart.

prompt: A program is run twice and prints a different address for the same variable each time. Is something wrong?
optionA: Yes; the same variable should always have the same address
optionB: No; where the program view is placed can differ between runs
optionC: Yes; the program is corrupting its own memory
optionD: No, but only because the machine was restarted
correctAnswerText: No; where the program view is placed can differ between runs
explanation: Nothing guarantees the same placement from one run to the next, and some systems deliberately vary it. An address is meaningful within a run rather than across runs.

prompt: A value is placed in the call-tied region during a function call. When is that memory released?
optionA: When the value is last used
optionB: When the program ends
optionC: When the memory is needed by something else
optionD: When the call returns
correctAnswerText: When the call returns
explanation: The release happens at the end of the call regardless of whether the value was still wanted. That automatic release is what the region is for.

prompt: In a language that does not reclaim memory automatically, a value is obtained in the longer-lived region and the program stops referring to it. When is that memory released?
optionA: Only when the program explicitly releases it
optionB: When the last reference to it disappears
optionC: When the enclosing call returns
optionD: Immediately, since nothing refers to it
correctAnswerText: Only when the program explicitly releases it
explanation: Without automatic reclamation, no longer referring to memory does not free it. The memory stays held for as long as the program runs unless it is released deliberately.

prompt: A function calls a second, which calls a third. While the third is running, how many calls are holding space?
optionA: One, the innermost
optionB: One, the outermost
optionC: Three, since all three are still in progress
optionD: None, until they return
correctAnswerText: Three, since all three are still in progress
explanation: A call that has not returned still holds its own space. All three are in progress at once, so all three are holding.

prompt: A function calls itself a thousand times before any call returns. What does that do to the call-tied region?
optionA: Only one call holds space, since it is the same function
optionB: A thousand calls hold space simultaneously, which may exhaust it
optionC: Space is released as each call is entered
optionD: Nothing, since the region grows without limit
correctAnswerText: A thousand calls hold space simultaneously, which may exhaust it
explanation: Being the same function does not merge the calls; each has its own space. The region is considerably smaller than memory as a whole, which is why depth exhausts it first.

prompt: In a language that reclaims memory automatically, a program stops referring to a large structure. What happens to the memory?
optionA: It stays held until the program ends
optionB: It is released the instant the last reference disappears
optionC: It must be released explicitly by the program
optionD: It becomes available again once the system notices nothing refers to it
correctAnswerText: It becomes available again once the system notices nothing refers to it
explanation: Automatic reclamation notices unreachable memory and takes it back, though not necessarily at the moment the last reference goes. The timing is the system decision rather than the program.

prompt: In a language that reclaims automatically, a program keeps every structure it has ever created in a list it never empties. Is that memory reclaimed?
optionA: No; the list still refers to them, so nothing is unreachable
optionB: Yes, since the program has finished using them
optionC: Yes, once memory runs short
optionD: No, because automatic reclamation does not work on lists
correctAnswerText: No; the list still refers to them, so nothing is unreachable
explanation: Reclamation acts on what nothing refers to, and the list refers to everything. This is how a language that reclaims automatically still runs out of memory.

prompt: In a language that does not reclaim automatically, a function obtains memory each time it runs and never releases it. The function is called once per request. The language does not reclaim automatically and the function releases nothing it obtains. What happens over a day?
optionA: Memory is reclaimed when each call returns
optionB: Memory is reclaimed when the request finishes
optionC: Memory held rises with every request and is never given back
optionD: Nothing; memory obtained once is reused on later calls
correctAnswerText: Memory held rises with every request and is never given back
explanation: The call returning releases the call-tied region and not memory obtained for an indefinite lifetime. One request is unnoticeable and a day of requests is not.

prompt: Programs on a machine together want more memory than the machine physically has. What happens?
optionA: The newest program is refused and stopped
optionB: Some of it is kept in storage and fetched back when needed, which is much slower
optionC: Every program is given an equal share and none exceeds it
optionD: The machine stops immediately
correctAnswerText: Some of it is kept in storage and fetched back when needed, which is much slower
explanation: Borrowing space from storage lets the machine keep going and costs a great deal of speed. Refusal comes later, if at all.

prompt: A machine short of memory becomes very slow, and a team checks and finds the processor is busy. Does that rule out memory as the cause?
optionA: Yes; a busy processor means the processor is the bottleneck
optionB: Yes; memory problems leave the processor idle
optionC: No, but only if the machine has one processor
optionD: No; moving memory to and from storage keeps the processor busy
correctAnswerText: No; moving memory to and from storage keeps the processor busy
explanation: The processor being busy is consistent with memory pressure rather than evidence against it. What it is busy doing is the question worth asking.

prompt: A machine becomes slow at everything at once — unrelated programs, the interface, commands that normally return instantly. Every program on the machine is affected rather than one, and nothing was deployed. Which cause fits?
optionA: Memory pressure, since it degrades everything on the machine rather than one program
optionB: A fault in one program, which is consuming the processor
optionC: A slow disk affecting one program
optionD: A network problem
correctAnswerText: Memory pressure, since it degrades everything on the machine rather than one program
explanation: A single program consuming the processor leaves other work slower and not uniformly unresponsive. Everything degrading together points at a resource everything depends on.

prompt: Two separate programs each hold a counter and one increments its own. Does the other see the change?
optionA: Yes, since both run on the same machine
optionB: Yes, if the two counters have the same name
optionC: No; each has its own memory unless sharing was arranged
optionD: Only after both programs finish
correctAnswerText: No; each has its own memory unless sharing was arranged
explanation: Separate programs see separate memory by default. Sharing between them is something that has to be set up deliberately.

prompt: A program is started twice, and each run keeps a list. One run adds an item. Does the other run see it?
optionA: Yes, since both are running the same program
optionB: No; the two runs are separate and have separate memory
optionC: Yes, since the list has the same name in both
optionD: Only if the two were started at the same moment
correctAnswerText: No; the two runs are separate and have separate memory
explanation: Sharing a program does not mean sharing memory. Each run is its own process with its own view of memory.

prompt: A team runs four copies of a service to handle more load, and finds that a value cached by one copy is not seen by the other three. The four copies are separate programs and no sharing was arranged between them. Why?
optionA: The cache is expiring too quickly
optionB: The four copies are interfering with one another
optionC: The value was never cached at all
optionD: Each copy has its own memory, so a cache in one is invisible to the rest
correctAnswerText: Each copy has its own memory, so a cache in one is invisible to the rest
explanation: This is the ordinary consequence of running separate copies, and it surprises teams because the code is identical. A cache shared between them has to live somewhere all four can reach.

prompt: A program reads a large file one line at a time, dealing with each line and keeping nothing. What decides how much memory it needs?
optionA: The size of the largest single line
optionB: The size of the whole file
optionC: The number of lines in the file
optionD: The time the program takes to run
correctAnswerText: The size of the largest single line
explanation: Only one line is held at any moment, so that is what has to fit. The total processed can be far larger than the memory available.

prompt: A program reads the same large file by loading all of it into a list first. What decides how much memory it needs now?
optionA: The size of the largest single line
optionB: The number of lines only
optionC: The size of the whole file
optionD: Nothing; the requirement is the same either way
correctAnswerText: The size of the whole file
explanation: Holding everything at once means everything has to fit. The two approaches process identical data and have completely different requirements.

prompt: A program processes ten gigabytes of records and runs comfortably on a machine with two gigabytes of memory. A colleague says this is impossible. The program holds one record at a time and discards each before reading the next. Is it possible?
optionA: No; ten gigabytes cannot be processed with two
optionB: Yes; what must fit is what is held at once rather than what is processed in total
optionC: Yes, but only because the records are compressed
optionD: Yes, but only if the machine borrows from storage
correctAnswerText: Yes; what must fit is what is held at once rather than what is processed in total
explanation: The total processed and the amount held simultaneously are different quantities, and only the second has to fit. Borrowing from storage is not needed here and would be slow if it were.

prompt: A program disappears with no message while doing memory-intensive work. What is one plausible explanation?
optionA: The program finished successfully
optionB: The program is still running but hidden
optionC: The user must have stopped it
optionD: The system stopped it because memory ran out
correctAnswerText: The system stopped it because memory ran out
explanation: A process stopped from outside because memory ran short leaves no message of its own. The silence is what makes this hard to recognise.

prompt: A program reports that it could not obtain memory and continues running in a reduced way. What has happened?
optionA: A request for memory was refused, and the program handled the refusal
optionB: The program was stopped by the system and restarted
optionC: The machine has no memory left at all
optionD: The program is about to be stopped
correctAnswerText: A request for memory was refused, and the program handled the refusal
explanation: A refused request is a different symptom from being stopped, and it is one the program can respond to. Being stopped from outside gives it no such opportunity.

prompt: A service disappears every few days with no message in its own log, and the machine log records that the system stopped it. The service own log ends mid-operation and the system log records the system stopping it. What does this indicate?
optionA: The service crashed and failed to log the crash
optionB: The service stopped itself deliberately
optionC: The system stopped it from outside, most likely because memory ran short
optionD: The machine restarted
correctAnswerText: The system stopped it from outside, most likely because memory ran short
explanation: A service that crashed would usually record something, and one stopped from outside cannot. The two logs together distinguish the cases.

prompt: A service memory use rises steadily over a week under constant load and never falls. What does that indicate?
optionA: Normal behaviour under sustained load
optionB: Something is being obtained repeatedly and never released
optionC: A cache filling up
optionD: Increasing traffic
correctAnswerText: Something is being obtained repeatedly and never released
explanation: Load is constant, so rising demand does not explain it. Growth that never levels off is the signature of memory that is never given back.

prompt: A service memory use rises quickly for two hours after each restart and then stays flat for days. A team plans to spend a week hunting a leak. Memory rises and then levels off rather than continuing to rise. What does the pattern indicate?
optionA: A leak that pauses when the machine is busy
optionB: A leak that is being partly reclaimed
optionC: Memory pressure from other programs
optionD: A cache filling to its limit, which is not a leak
correctAnswerText: A cache filling to its limit, which is not a leak
explanation: A leak does not stop. Levelling off is what a bounded cache does, and the week would have been spent looking for something that is not there.

prompt: A program fails within a second of starting, on an input of five items, on a machine with plenty of free memory. It uses a function that calls itself. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The function is calling itself without ever stopping, exhausting the call-tied region
optionB: The machine is short of memory
optionC: The input is too large
optionD: Memory is leaking over time
correctAnswerText: The function is calling itself without ever stopping, exhausting the call-tied region
explanation: Failing at once on five items rules out both a shortage and a leak, since neither would act that fast on that little. A call chain with no end exhausts a small region very quickly.

prompt: A program processing a list of three items fails immediately, while the machine reports fifteen gigabytes free. A colleague proposes adding memory. The input is three items and fifteen gigabytes are free, so the machine is not short of memory. What is the fault?
optionA: A memory leak that has consumed the available memory
optionB: The machine is short of memory despite what it reports
optionC: A call chain with no end, which exhausts the small call-tied region regardless of free memory
optionD: The three items are unusually large
correctAnswerText: A call chain with no end, which exhausts the small call-tied region regardless of free memory
explanation: Adding memory would not touch the region that is actually full, which is sized separately and is far smaller. The failure being instant on three items is what points at depth.

prompt: One program on a machine is slow and everything else is normal. Does memory pressure explain it?
optionA: Yes; the program must be the one short of memory
optionB: No; memory pressure would slow the whole machine rather than one program
optionC: Yes; other programs may have enough memory
optionD: It cannot be decided
correctAnswerText: No; memory pressure would slow the whole machine rather than one program
explanation: Borrowing from storage affects everything competing for memory. A single slow program points somewhere within that program.

prompt: A machine becomes slow at the same time each night. A team suspects memory pressure. Every program on the machine slows together at that time and a large report job runs then. What would confirm it?
optionA: Checking whether the report job has grown longer
optionB: Checking whether the processor is busy at that time
optionC: Restarting the machine before the report job runs
optionD: Checking whether memory in use rises at that time and storage activity rises with it
correctAnswerText: Checking whether memory in use rises at that time and storage activity rises with it
explanation: The processor being busy is consistent with memory pressure and does not confirm it. Memory in use rising together with storage activity is what distinguishes it from anything else.

prompt: A team doubles the memory on a machine that was slow, and it becomes fast. They conclude the cause was memory pressure. Doubling the memory removed the need to borrow from storage, and nothing else about the machine changed. Is the conclusion sound?
optionA: Yes; the change addressed one thing and the symptom went with it
optionB: No; correlation is not causation and nothing has been shown
optionC: No; the machine may have been restarted at the same time
optionD: Yes, but only if the load was measured before and after
correctAnswerText: Yes; the change addressed one thing and the symptom went with it
explanation: A single change followed by the symptom disappearing is genuine evidence, and this is what a controlled change looks like. Refusing to conclude anything from it is as unreasoning as concluding without it.

prompt: A service is slow and using far more memory than expected. A team adds memory and it stays slow, while the memory in use rises to fill the new space as well. Memory in use expands to fill whatever is provided, which is what a leak does and a genuine requirement does not. What does that indicate?
optionA: The service genuinely needs even more memory
optionB: The added memory was not configured correctly
optionC: Something is holding memory it does not need, so more memory is consumed rather than helping
optionD: The slowness has a cause unrelated to memory
correctAnswerText: Something is holding memory it does not need, so more memory is consumed rather than helping
explanation: A real requirement would have been satisfied and levelled off. Expanding to fill whatever is available is what unbounded retention does, and adding memory postpones it rather than fixing it.

prompt: A program is slow and a team finds it is using only a small fraction of the available memory. A colleague concludes memory cannot be involved. The program holds very little at once and repeatedly reads data that no longer fits in the fastest layers of memory. Is the conclusion sound?
optionA: Yes; low memory use rules memory out entirely
optionB: No; how memory is accessed can matter even when the amount used is small
optionC: Yes, unless the machine is also running other programs
optionD: No; the program must actually be using more than reported
correctAnswerText: No; how memory is accessed can matter even when the amount used is small
explanation: Running out is one memory problem and access patterns are another. A program touching a large range unpredictably is slow while using very little.

prompt: A value is expensive to compute and is needed on every request. The machine has ample free memory and the value never changes. The value never changes and memory is not constrained. Should it be held or recomputed?
optionA: Recomputed, since holding values risks running out of memory
optionB: Recomputed, since held values become stale
optionC: Held, but only for a few minutes at a time
optionD: Held, since it never changes and memory is not the scarce resource here
correctAnswerText: Held, since it never changes and memory is not the scarce resource here
explanation: Both conditions that argue against holding are absent: it cannot go stale and memory is plentiful. Recomputing would pay the cost on every request for nothing.

prompt: A team caches every result the service has ever computed, with no limit. The machine has ample memory today. A cache with no limit grows with every distinct request and there is no point at which it stops. What follows?
optionA: It will eventually exhaust memory, however much there is, because nothing bounds it
optionB: It is safe while the machine has ample memory
optionC: It is safe, since caches are reclaimed automatically
optionD: It will level off once the common requests are cached
correctAnswerText: It will eventually exhaust memory, however much there is, because nothing bounds it
explanation: Levelling off requires the set of distinct requests to be bounded, which nothing has established. A limit on size or age is what turns this from a leak into a cache.

prompt: A program can hold an entire dataset in memory and answer instantly, or read from storage each time and answer slowly. The dataset is four gigabytes, the machine has three, and holding it would force the machine to borrow from storage continuously. Holding four gigabytes on a three-gigabyte machine means borrowing from storage for every access. What follows?
optionA: Holding it is faster, since memory is faster than storage
optionB: Holding it is faster, since the system manages the borrowing efficiently
optionC: Holding it would be slower than reading from storage deliberately, since the borrowing happens anyway and unpredictably
optionD: The two approaches perform identically
correctAnswerText: Holding it would be slower than reading from storage deliberately, since the borrowing happens anyway and unpredictably
explanation: The intended benefit disappears once the data does not fit, and the borrowing is less efficient than reading deliberately would be. Reading a working subset into memory is the arrangement that gets the benefit.

prompt: A team must choose between holding a value that becomes stale after a minute, and recomputing it each time at a cost of fifty milliseconds. Requests arrive a thousand times a second and a stale value would show a customer an out-of-date balance. A stale balance is shown to a customer, while recomputing costs fifty milliseconds per request. What should decide?
optionA: The request rate, since a thousand a second makes recomputing impossible
optionB: Whether showing a balance up to a minute out of date is acceptable, since that is the cost of holding it
optionC: The recomputation cost, since fifty milliseconds is small
optionD: Neither; the value should be held and refreshed every second
correctAnswerText: Whether showing a balance up to a minute out of date is acceptable, since that is the cost of holding it
explanation: The rate makes holding attractive and does not settle whether staleness is tolerable, which is a question about what the customer is being shown. Refreshing every second is a reasonable compromise that the stem gives no grounds to prefer.

prompt: A service holds a large structure for the whole of its run because releasing and rebuilding it is complicated. It is used for one minute in every hour. The structure occupies memory for fifty-nine minutes in every hour during which nothing uses it. What is the trade?
optionA: Nothing; holding it is obviously correct
optionB: Nothing; rebuilding it is obviously correct
optionC: Whether the structure can be made smaller
optionD: Memory held almost all the time against the complexity of building it when needed
correctAnswerText: Memory held almost all the time against the complexity of building it when needed
explanation: Both sides are real: the memory is genuinely wasted and the rebuilding is genuinely complicated. Which wins depends on whether that memory is needed for anything else.

prompt: A system provides a pool of twenty connections. Code takes one for each request and returns it when finished. One path through the code takes a connection and returns early without returning it. Connections are taken from a fixed pool and this path never returns the one it took. What happens over time?
optionA: The pool empties and later requests wait for a connection that never comes
optionB: Nothing; unreturned connections are reclaimed automatically
optionC: The pool grows to meet demand
optionD: Only the affected path fails, and other requests are unaffected
correctAnswerText: The pool empties and later requests wait for a connection that never comes
explanation: This is a leak in a different resource and behaves exactly the same way. Every request eventually suffers, not only the ones taking the faulty path.

prompt: A program opens files and relies on them being closed when it ends. It runs for months and opens thousands of files a day. The limit on open files applies while the program runs and the program does not end for months. What is the difficulty?
optionA: Nothing; files are always closed when a program ends
optionB: The files will be closed automatically when memory runs short
optionC: The limit is reached long before the program ends, so relying on that cleanup fails
optionD: The program will slow down but continue
correctAnswerText: The limit is reached long before the program ends, so relying on that cleanup fails
explanation: Cleanup at exit is real and arrives far too late for a program that does not exit. This is the same shape as memory obtained and never released.

prompt: A team is told that a resource is released automatically when the code holding it goes out of scope. They wrap every use in that construct and one path exits by throwing an error before reaching it. The construct releases the resource when scope is left, and an error leaves scope in the same way a normal return does. What happens on that path?
optionA: The resource leaks, since the error skipped the release
optionB: The resource is still released, since leaving scope by an error is still leaving scope
optionC: The resource leaks, since errors bypass automatic cleanup
optionD: The behaviour depends on the type of error
correctAnswerText: The resource is still released, since leaving scope by an error is still leaving scope
explanation: This is why the construct exists rather than a manual release at the end of a block. The path that would leak under a manual release is exactly the one it protects.

prompt: A team must decide whether to give each request its own connection or share one across all requests. Connections are limited and a shared one would serialise every request behind a single point. Connections are a bounded resource and sharing one forces requests to queue. What follows?
optionA: One per request, since that is simplest
optionB: One shared, since connections are limited
optionC: One per request, with the limit raised as needed
optionD: Neither extreme fits; a bounded pool shared among requests is what the constraint implies
correctAnswerText: Neither extreme fits; a bounded pool shared among requests is what the constraint implies
explanation: One per request exhausts the bound and one shared destroys concurrency, and the constraint rules out both. A pool sized to the bound is the arrangement the two facts point at.
